If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipse very closely. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, were to describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity at any point *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* applied to the diameter *AB* of a circle. Therefore, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at individual points of *Ba* are, very closely, to the velocities at corresponding points of the length *BA*, as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate applied to a circle or ellipse described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipse very closely. Since the resistance is assumed to be proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the midpoint *O*; and the ellipse *BRVSa*, described with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will equal the figure *BKVT a*, and the rectangle *Aa* x *BO* equal to it, very closely. Therefore, *Aa* x *BO* is to *OV* x *BO* as the area of this ellipse is to *OV* x *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semicircle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 is to 7 approximately: And therefore $\frac{7}{11} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be nearly a parabola having vertex *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore will be equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ & *OV* very closely. The rectangle under $\frac{1}{2} Ba$ & *Aa* is therefore equal to the rectangle under $\frac{2}{3} Ba$ & *OV*, and therefore *OV* is equal to $\frac{3}{4} Aa$: and therefore the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as $\frac{3}{4} Aa$ is to the length of the pendulum.

Galen agrees with Plato; but Hipparchus says that rays extended from the eyes to bodies touch them as if by a certain palpitation, rendering their perception to the sight. 4 The other distinction between the Old and New Testaments is established in figures: the former, in the absence of the truth, showed only an image and a shadow instead of the body; the latter exhibits the present truth and a solid body. And mention of this is made almost everywhere the New Testament is opposed to the Old; yet its treatment is more extensive in the epistle to the Hebrews than anywhere else. There, the Apostle argues against those who thought that the observances of the Mosaic Law could not be abolished without dragging with them the ruin of the entire religion. To refute this error, he takes up <margin>Psal. 110. b. 4</margin> what had been predicted by the Prophet concerning the priesthood of Christ. For since an eternal priesthood is bestowed upon him, it is certain that the priesthood was abolished where successors were substituted for one another daily. He proves, moreover, that the institution of this new priest prevails because <margin>Heb. 7. b. 11. c. 19. & 9. c. 9. & 10. a. 1</margin> it is established by an oath. He adds afterwards that in that translation of the priesthood, there is also a change of the Testament. And he confirms that this was necessary by reason, because such was the weakness of the Law that it could bring nothing to perfection. Then he proceeds to what that weakness was, namely, that it had external justices of the flesh which could not make their worshippers perfect according to the conscience, and that it could neither blot out sins nor procure true holiness through the sacrifices of beasts. He concludes, therefore, that there was a shadow in the very things of future goods, not a living likeness of the realities; and that it therefore had no function other than to be an introduction into the better hope which is exhibited in the Gospel. Here it must be seen in what part the Legal covenant is compared with the Evangelical covenant, the ministry of Christ with the Mosaic. For if the comparison pertained to the substance of the promises, a great discord would exist between the two Testaments; but since the state of the question leads us elsewhere, we must aim to find the truth. Let us, therefore, set in the middle the covenant that God sanctioned once, which is eternal and will never perish. The fulfillment of that covenant, from which it finally has it that it is established and ratified, is Christ. While such a confirmation is awaited, the Lord prescribes ceremonies through Moses, which are as it were the solemn symbols of confirmation. This was coming into contention: whether the ceremonies ordained in the Law ought to yield to Christ. These, even though they were only accidents of the covenant, or at least accessions and annexes, and (as the common people say) accessories; yet because they were instruments for administering it, they have the name of the covenant, just as it is accustomed to be given to other <term>sacraments</term> <gloss>sacred signs</gloss>. Therefore, in sum, the Old Testament is called here the solemn method of confirming the covenant, comprised of ceremonies and sacrifices. Since there is nothing solid underneath, unless one passes further, the Apostle contends that it had to be antiquated and abrogated, so that place might be given to Christ, the sponsor and mediator of a better Testament, through whom eternal sanctification has been acquired once for all for the elect, and transgressions have been obliterated, which remained under the Law. But if you are displeased, take it thus: there was an old Testament of the Lord, which was delivered wrapped up in the shadowy and ineffective observation of ceremonies. And it was therefore temporary, because it was, as it were, in suspense, until it might be supported by a firm and substantial confirmation. But then finally it became new and eternal, after it was consecrated and stabilized by the blood of Christ. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to be of that light, nevertheless are; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form from the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man constitute so much that he cannot think without them, are also of the light of the world. The light of heaven, however, is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and attributes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he has perception only of those things which are of the light of the world, but not of those which are of the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the universal heaven is in that light. This light—namely, the light of heaven—is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Things which form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception at all, for those things which belong to the light of the world have life from that source. Between these lights—or between those things which are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world—there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual man; that is, when the former serves the latter. And the things which then exist in the light of the world are representative of those things which are in the light of heaven.

*To correct is to take the corrected.* If a man is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections of yours too; it is situated within the things themselves, not within you. Now, in this case, a physician must consider nothing more than that the poison should be removed. This must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood regarding all other things equally, namely, that a similar separation is necessary. That not having been done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your turns, or a greater kindness of heaven favors you. Now, therefore, if that true foundation is required which removes the poison, how does Alchemy provide it?
